episodes.205341: A slow moving cluster of heavy showers and embedded thunderstorms dumped 3-6 inches of rainfall over a 3-6 hour period in a portion of northwest Alabama.  The heaviest rain fell in eastern Colbert County which resulted in flooding and one water rescue in the Leighton area.
episodes.205461: Strong storms developed near the Watertown area, with hail to 1 inch diameter. A brief funnel cloud was spotted near the town of Waverly.
episodes.205898: A shortwave trough interacted with a southerly monsoon moisture and an unstable airmass to produce afternoon to early evening thunderstorms.
episodes.205900: A shortwave trough interacted with a southerly monsoon moisture and an unstable airmass to produce afternoon to early evening thunderstorms.
episodes.206989: Thunderstorms developed over southwest North Dakota in an area of elevated instability. One storm became severe to the south of Mott in Hettinger County, producing half-dollar diameter hail.
episodes.207039: Mid-level high pressure centered over NW AZ resulted an easterly steering flow across much of the southern half of AZ. Thunderstorms initially developed over the Mogollon Rim during the early to mid afternoon hours and were steered west-southwestward into the lower elevations of south-central AZ with additional activity developing from outflow boundaries. The combination of MLCAPE values peaking at around 500 J/kg and DCAPE values near 2000 J/kg resulted in a very favorable environment for strong to severe downburst wind gusts.
episodes.207316: Around 10 AM PDT on Tuesday, September 2, 2025, a decaying complex of showers and thunderstorms moved over the Carmichael area of the Sacramento metropolitan area in Sacramento County. It was determined that this caused a downburst of strong straight-line winds. Sporadic wind damage to trees and powerlines was noted along with several large mature trees that were uprooted and fell into homes. The damage swath was 2.5 miles long and 1.5 miles wide from American River College, northeast in the vicinity of a line from East Lawn Mortuary to Mercy San Juan Medical Center. Peak wind speeds were estimated around 70 miles per hour.
episodes.207570: Enhanced trade winds brought an increase in tropical moisture. Additionally, instability aloft increased due to the vicinity of an upper-level low. These features fuel strong showers and thunderstorms, causing flooding.
episodes.207760: On the morning of September 1, 2025, a mesoscale vorticity maximum advancing into eastern Nebraska provided the necessary forcing for lift, resulting in a persistent band of moderate to heavy showers. The concurrent presence of a 20-25 knot low-level jet significantly enhanced the inflow of a very moist, albeit weakly unstable, air mass. This dynamic led to radar-estimated rainfall rates reaching 2 to 3 inches per hour in localized areas. Overall, radar indicated rainfall totals pushed 4 to 6 inches across portions of eastern Nebraska, specifically impacting Lancaster, Seward, Saunders, and Saline counties. These high totals were validated by public reports, including a maximum of 5.51 inches received four miles northwest of Dorchester, Nebraska. The heavy precipitation initiated flooding concerns, including flash flooding in Dorchester, where reports indicated water estimated at 2 to 4 inches deep over roadways in some locations. Runoff from the event led to continued hydrological concerns even after the rainfall subsided, with emergency management reporting water over numerous roads south and west of Milford, NE, at 6:35 AM CST. Additionally, river flooding was recorded, affecting the North Oak Creek at Valparaiso, which crested at a minor flood stage of 20.21 feet at 5:30 AM CST on September 1st, and the Big Blue River at Crete, NE, which crested at a minor flood stage of 21.30 feet at 12:30 AM CST on September 2nd.||A second area of concern was focused in Saunders County, particularly along the Wahoo Creek. The severity was highlighted at 12:45 PM CST on September 1, 2025, when a public photograph showed water levels nearly reaching the top I-beam of the School Street bridge over Wahoo Creek in Weston, NE. The impact continued into the evening, with an NWS employee reporting at 5:45 PM CST that water was over County Road J near County Road 15, located two miles south-southeast of Wahoo, Nebraska. The Wahoo Creek at Ithaca also experienced flooding, cresting at a minor flood stage of 19.55 feet at 6:15 AM CST on September 2nd, 2025.
episodes.207834: A strong ridge over the region resulted in a heat risk through the middle of the week, and a return of monsoonal moisture allowed for thunderstorms the develop, mainly over the mountains and deserts throughout the rest of the week.
episodes.207867: A push of monsoon moisture fueled isolated thunderstorms for several days. A few produced severe weather and flash flooding.
episodes.207962: Scattered thunderstorms developed across portions of Mississippi during the afternoon of September 2nd. Some were strong with gusty winds.

On the morning of September 1, 2025, intense thunderstorms generated heavy rainfall and subsequent flooding concerns across portions of eastern Nebraska, specifically Seward County. Radar estimated total rainfall for the event ranged from 3 to 6 inches. These assessments were strongly supported by public rainfall reports, which documented significant totals, including 5.51 inches four miles northwest of Dorchester, NE, 4.43 inches five miles north of Dorchester, NE, and 3.97 inches three miles west-northwest of Milford, NE. The resultant runoff from this excessive precipitation led to riverine flooding in Seward County along the Big Blue River near Crete, NE. The river officially entered flood stage at 8:30 PM CST on September 1, 2025, and reached its maximum height, or crest, of 21.30 feet���a level corresponding to minor flood stage���at 12:30 AM CST on September 2, 2025. The Big Blue River subsequently receded and fell below flood stage at 4:30 AM CST on September 2, 2025.
